Radom Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Radom, Poland

Demolished. Jews lived in Radom from at least the 16th century, though official community status only formed in the 1830s. A cholera epidemic in 1831 prompted the community to establish an emergency burial ground, recognized in 1837 as Radom's permanent Jewish cemetery and expanded three times by 1911 to roughly 5 hectares. By 1938, nearly 25,000 Jews - almost 30% of Radom's population - called the city home. The cemetery was devastated during World War II, its stones repurposed for construction and victims of the Radom Ghetto buried in mass graves; it remained in intermittent use until 1951, including the postwar reburial of bodies exhumed from nearby forced-labor camps. Since 1989, restoration has rebuilt its wall and gate, added a lapidarium and mausoleum honoring Holocaust victims, and recovered tombstones - the oldest dating to 1837 - many mounted along its main path and walls.
